entry: French professional football club based in Paris, founded in 1970 through the merger of Paris FC and Stade Saint-Germain. It plays in [[Ligue 1]] at the Parc des Princes and is the most successful club in French football, with 60 major trophies, including two [[UEFA Champions League]] titles. Qatar Sports Investments (QSI) has been its majority owner since 2011. Other sections include [[Handball]], [[Judo]] and [[Esports|esports]].

Property of an [[Integer|integer]] as even or odd. An integer is even if it is divisible by 2 and odd if it is not; for example, −4, 0 and 82 are even, while −7, 5 and 23 are odd. Parity applies only to integers, not to fractions or decimals such as 1⁄2 or 7.2742. Zero is even, and any two consecutive integers have opposite parity. In the decimal system an integer is odd if its last digit is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, and in the binary system it is odd if its last digit is 1. Parity is a special case of [[Modular arithmetic]]: modulo 2, the even and odd numbers form a field with two elements. When the quotient of two integers is itself an integer, it is even if and only if the dividend has more factors of two than the divisor.

Area of natural, semi-natural or planted land set aside for recreation or the protection of wildlife. Urban parks are green spaces inside towns and cities, while national and country parks lie in the countryside. Many have fields for [[Baseball]] and [[Football|football]], paved areas for [[Basketball]], and [[Trail|trails]] for walking. In large parks, camping in tents may be allowed with a permit, and some parks have rules against open fires. Medieval English deer parks were walled preserves used by the aristocracy for game hunting. From the 16th century, landscaped parks were laid out around country houses, and as cities became crowded, private hunting grounds became places for the public. With the [[Industrial Revolution]], parks were set aside to preserve a sense of nature in towns, and sport became a major use. Areas of outstanding natural beauty were also set aside as national parks to prevent uncontrolled development from spoiling them.

South Korean army officer and president (r. 1963–79). Park seized power in the May 16 coup of 1961 and, after two years as junta chairman, was elected president in 1963.A firm anti-communist, he kept close ties with the [[United States]] and sent South Korean troops to fight in Vietnam. His government introduced economic reforms that led to rapid industrialization, known as the Miracle on the Han River, and supported family companies such as [[Samsung]]. In 1972 he declared martial law after a self-coup and introduced the authoritarian Yushin Constitution, after which he repressed political opposition and dissent and exerted much control over the media. He was assassinated in 1979 by Kim Jae-gyu, director of the KCIA, following the Busan–Masan Uprising. Assessments of his legacy are divided: some credit him with sustained [[Economic growth|economic growth]], while critics point to authoritarian rule and its cost to [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]] and [[Human rights|human rights]].

Act of stopping and leaving a vehicle, usually unoccupied. Parking on one or both sides of a road is often permitted, sometimes with restrictions. Public parking is managed by local government authorities, while private parking is owned by an entity that may restrict it to customers, employees or residents. On-street parking may be parallel, angled or perpendicular, and it can act as inexpensive traffic calming by reducing the effective width of the street. Restrictions may include waiting prohibitions, time limits, payment at a meter, or permit zones. Off-street parking lots and garages are either structured or surface. Cars are typically stationary about 95 percent of the time, and in many North American city centers half or more of all [[Urban area|urban land]] is devoted to car parking. The first public parking garage for motor vehicles was opened in [[Boston]] on May 24, 1898.

Progressive neurodegenerative disease, primarily of the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. The loss of [[Dopamine|dopamine]]-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the brainstem causes the motor symptoms, known as parkinsonism: tremor, bradykinesia (slowness in initiating movement), rigidity and postural instability. Non-motor symptoms include sleep abnormalities, loss of smell, [[Depression (mood)|depression]], cognitive impairment, psychosis and anxiety. Misfolded alpha-synuclein proteins aggregate into Lewy bodies. No single cause is known; genetic and environmental factors interact. Diagnosis is based primarily on signs and symptoms identified through neurological examination, and [[Medical imaging|medical imaging]] such as PET scanning can support it. Onset is typically in people over 60, and the condition affects about one percent of that group. No cure is known. Levodopa, MAO-B inhibitors and dopamine agonists improve symptoms initially but become less effective as the disease progresses, and deep brain stimulation is used for severe motor symptoms. [[Life expectancy|Life expectancy]] is reduced.

Law-making body, or [[Legislature|legislature]], of a state. A parliament generally represents the electorate, makes laws and oversees the executive government through hearings and inquiries. The term is commonly used in current or former monarchies, and a parliament is the institutional form of parliamentary systems. Medieval parliamentary gatherings established that monarchs were subject to law. The Cortes of León in 1188 and an English parliament in 1265 summoned representatives of common people, and the English body developed into the House of Commons. In 1283 the [[Catalonia|Corts of Catalonia]] became Europe's first parliament officially recognized as a legislative body. The [[Glorious Revolution]] of 1688 established the primacy of parliamentary sovereignty in Britain. Expansion of [[Suffrage|suffrage]] in the 19th and 20th centuries led many parliaments to become democratically elected.

Supreme legislative body of the United Kingdom, meeting at the [[Palace of Westminster]] in London. It is bicameral, with the elected House of Commons, which has 650 members from single-member constituencies, and the [[House of Lords]], with the sovereign as a third constitutional element. The Commons has legislative primacy: under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords can generally delay, rather than permanently block, legislation. The present Parliament was created on 1 January 1801 under the Acts of Union 1800.

Creative work that imitates, comments on or mocks its subject through satirical or ironic imitation. The subject is often an original work or an aspect of it, but may also be a real person, event or movement. Parody occurs in [[Literature|literature]], music, theater, television, film, animation and gaming. The critic John Gross places parody between pastiche and [[Burlesque|burlesque]]. Denis Diderot's *Encyclopédie* distinguished the two: a good parody is a fine amusement, while burlesque is a miserable buffoonery. In [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], a *parodia* was a narrative poem imitating the style of epics but treating light, satirical or mock-heroic subjects. According to [[Aristotle]], Hegemon of Thasos invented the form by slightly altering well-known poems. In the 2nd century CE, [[Lucian]] of Samosata parodied travel texts; his *True History* is sometimes described as the first science fiction. [[Buster Keaton]] shorts mocked the moralistic melodramas of the 1910s.

Bird of the order Psittaciformes, with a strong curved beak, upright stance and clawed feet. Roughly 410 species in 101 genera are classified in four families, found mostly in tropical and subtropical regions. The greatest diversity is in [[South America]] and [[Australasia]]. Along with corvids, parrots are among the most intelligent birds, and the ability of some species to imitate human [[Speech|speech]] adds to their popularity as pets. Most parrots eat seeds, nuts, fruit, buds and other plant material, and almost all nest in tree hollows. Parrots have a higher aggregate extinction risk (IUCN Red List Index) than any other comparable bird group. Trapping for the pet trade, [[Hunting|hunting]], habitat loss and competition from [[Invasive species|invasive species]] have diminished wild populations. About 50 million parrots, half of all parrots, lived in captivity as of 2021. Molecular studies suggest that the order evolved about 59 million years ago in [[Gondwana]].

Unit of length used in astronomy, equal to about 3.26 [[Light-year|light-years]]. The parsec measures distances to objects outside the [[Solar System]]; it is equal to about 206,265 astronomical units (au), or 30.9 trillion kilometers. It is defined as the distance at which 1 au subtends an angle of one arcsecond, a relation derived from [[Parallax|parallax]] and [[Trigonometry|trigonometry]]. The nearest star, [[Proxima Centauri]], is about 1.3 parsecs (4.2 light-years) from the Sun, while the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] lies at over 700,000 parsecs (2,283,000 ly). The word was coined by Herbert Hall Turner in 1913 as a shortened form of "parallax of one arcsecond". Multiples include kiloparsecs (kpc), megaparsecs (Mpc) and gigaparsecs (Gpc). In August 2015 the International Astronomical Union (IAU) passed Resolution B2, which mentions an explicit definition of the parsec as exactly 648000/π au.

Ethnoreligious community in the Indian subcontinent, descended from Persian Zoroastrians. Its ancestors, citizens of the [[Sasanian Empire]], fled persecution after the Arab conquest of Iran in the 7th century and settled in [[Gujarat]], where the Rajput king of Sanjan granted them refuge. According to the 16th-century epic *Qissa-i Sanjan*, a Parsi priest added sugar to a vessel of milk to show that the settlers would blend in. Parsis are the elder of India's two [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrian]] communities and are distinct from Iranis. Parsis became highly influential in trade, industry, culture and philanthropy. Icons include Jamsetji Tata and Homi Bhabha.

Flowering plant of the family [[Apiaceae]], cultivated as a herb and vegetable. Garden parsley (*Petroselinum crispum*) is native to [[Greece]], the Balkans, [[Algeria]] and Morocco, and has been naturalized elsewhere in Europe. It is believed to have been originally grown in Sardinia, and according to historical horticultural sources it was brought to England in 1548, although literary evidence suggests it was used there in the [[Middle Ages]]. The name derives from Greek *petroselinon*, meaning rock-celery. Curly-leaf parsley is often used as a garnish, while flat-leaf parsley is preferred by many chefs for its stronger flavor. Root parsley is eaten as a vegetable in soups and stews in central, eastern and southern Europe. Parsley seeds are toxic and their use should be avoided. Parsley is the main ingredient of Italian salsa verde, and parsley sauce is a cream sauce used in British cuisine.

Root vegetable closely related to [[Carrot|carrot]] and [[Parsley|parsley]]. The parsnip (*Pastinaca sativa*) is a biennial, usually grown as an annual, native to [[Eurasia]]. Its cream-colored taproot becomes sweeter after winter [[Frost|frosts]]. It has been used as a vegetable since antiquity and was cultivated by the Romans, and it was a sweetener before cane [[Sugar|sugar]] reached Europe. European settlers introduced it to the Americas, where it became a common weed in [[North America]]. All parts of the plant contain furanocoumarins that can cause photodermatitis after contact with sunlight, and contact with the eyes can potentially blind. Parsnips are usually cooked, and their flesh is sweeter than carrots. They contain potassium, vitamins, antioxidants and dietary fiber. Parsnips grow best in deep, stone-free soil, and canker is the most serious of their diseases. Carolus Linnaeus described the species in his 1753 work *Species Plantarum*.

Form of [[Asexual reproduction|asexual reproduction]] in which an embryo develops without fertilization. In animals, it means the development of an embryo from an unfertilized egg. It occurs naturally in some plants and animals and in a few other [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], such as [[Oomycete|oomycetes]], and has been induced artificially in some mammals. Normal egg cells form through [[Meiosis|meiosis]] and are haploid, but haploid offspring are usually non-viable, so parthenogenetic offspring usually have the diploid number of [[Chromosome|chromosomes]]. Some species, such as bdelloid rotifers, reproduce only this way.In animals, the production of female offspring this way is called thelytoky, found among [[Aphid|aphids]].

Former temple on the [[Acropolis of Athens|Athenian Acropolis]], Greece, dedicated to [[Athena]]. Its sculptures are considered among the high points of classical Greek art. It was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persian invaders in the [[Greco-Persian Wars]]. Construction began in 447 BC, when the [[Delian League]] was at its peak, and was completed in 438 BC. The architects were Iktinos and Callicrates, and [[Phidias]] oversaw the sculpture. In the final decade of the 6th century AD it became a Christian church, and after the Ottoman conquest in the mid-15th century a mosque. A Venetian bomb hit the Ottoman munitions store inside it during the 1687 siege of the Acropolis, and the explosion severely damaged it. From 1800 to 1803 the 7th Earl of Elgin removed many of the surviving sculptures, now known as the Elgin Marbles. Restoration projects have been undertaken since 1975.

Iranian empire (247 BC–224 AD), also called the Arsacid Empire. Its founder, Arsaces I, led the Parni tribe in conquering Parthia, a region of northeastern Iran that was then a satrapy under [[Seleucid Empire|Seleucid]] rule. Mithridates I (r. c. 171–132 BC) greatly expanded the empire by seizing Media and Mesopotamia. At its height it stretched from the Euphrates to present-day [[Afghanistan]] and western Pakistan. Located on the [[Silk Road]] between the Roman Empire and the [[Han dynasty]] of China, it became a center of trade. Its rulers were titled "King of Kings", claiming the inheritance of the [[Achaemenid Empire]]. The Parthians destroyed the army of [[Marcus Licinius Crassus|Crassus]] at Carrhae in 53 BC. Frequent civil wars among Parthian contenders proved more dangerous than foreign invasion. In 224 AD Ardashir I, ruler of Istakhr, killed the last Arsacid ruler, Artabanus IV, and founded the [[Sasanian Empire]].

Derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one variable, with the others held constant. It measures the rate of change of the function in the direction of that variable, and it is defined as a limit. If all partial derivatives exist and are continuous near a point, the function is termed a C1 function there. Partial derivatives are used in [[Vector calculus]] and [[Differential geometry]]. Mixed second partial derivatives can be exchanged when they are continuous, by Clairaut's theorem. The symbol ∂ was first used by Marquis de Condorcet in 1770 for partial differences. The modern notation was created by [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] in 1786, although he later abandoned it, and [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]] reintroduced the symbol in 1841. In statistical mechanics, the partial derivative of f with respect to x, holding y and z constant, is written (∂f/∂x)y,z.

Equation relating a multivariable function to one or more of its [[Partial derivative|partial derivatives]]. Explicit formulas for its solutions are usually impossible to write down, so much research concerns numerical approximation by computers. Pure mathematics studies qualitative features such as existence, uniqueness, regularity and stability. Ordinary differential equations are a subclass, corresponding to functions of a single variable. PDEs are fundamental to the modern understanding of sound, [[Heat|heat]], diffusion, electrostatics, electrodynamics, [[Fluid dynamics]], elasticity, general relativity and [[Quantum mechanics]]. They are also the fundamental tool in the proof of the [[Poincaré conjecture]] from geometric topology. Laplace's equation is among the most important examples; functions that satisfy it are called harmonic. No universal theory of PDEs exists, and specialist knowledge is divided among distinct subfields.

Separate part of a larger system, in the physical sciences. Particles range from subatomic particles such as the [[Electron|electron]], through microscopic particles such as [[Atom|atoms]] and [[Molecule|molecules]], to macroscopic particles such as powders and granular materials. In some fields a particle is a small localized object described by properties such as volume, density or mass. Physics uses the concept to simplify models; a baseball can be idealized as a rigid smooth sphere, reducing its flight to [[Ballistics|ballistics]]. Massive particles move more slowly than light, while the [[Photon|photon]] is massless. The mass of atoms is concentrated in their nuclei, made of [[Proton|protons]] and neutrons, which each have over 1800 times more mass than electrons. Microscopic and subatomic particles are studied in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], which includes wave–particle duality.

Machine that uses electromagnetic fields to propel ions to very high speeds and energies. Small accelerators are used in [[Particle physics|particle physics]] research and as synchrotron light sources for [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter physics]]. Smaller ones are used in particle therapy, medical radioisotope production, semiconductor ion implantation and measurements of rare isotopes such as radiocarbon. The [[Large Hadron Collider]] near [[Geneva]], operated by [[CERN]], accelerates two beams of protons to 6.5 TeV and collides them head-on at 13 TeV. Of the more than 30,000 accelerators worldwide, about 44% are for radiotherapy and 41% for ion implantation. Electrostatic accelerators, such as the Van de Graaff generator, are limited by the voltage at which electrical breakdown occurs. Electrodynamic accelerators use changing fields, so particles can pass through the same field repeatedly; this class was first developed in the 1920s. Rolf Widerøe, Gustav Ising, Leó Szilárd, Max Steenbeck and [[Ernest Lawrence]] are considered pioneers of this field.

Device used to detect, track and identify ionizing particles, also called a radiation detector. Detected particles include those from nuclear decay, [[Cosmic ray|cosmic radiation]] and reactions in a [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerator]]. Detectors can measure a particle's energy, momentum, spin, charge and type, not merely its presence. Most are ionization detectors, such as gaseous and semiconductor detectors, or scintillation detectors; others use [[Cherenkov radiation|Čerenkov radiation]] or transition radiation. A primary signal, such as ionization of gas, electron-hole pairs in semiconductors or light in scintillators, is amplified and analyzed. Geiger counters, ionization chambers and dosimeters are widely used for radiation protection. Detectors in modern particle physics are layered, "much like an onion". At [[CERN]], the [[Large Hadron Collider]] has the ATLAS, CMS, ALICE and LHCb detectors, and the [[Tevatron]] had the CDF and D0 detectors.

The 1947 division of British India into two independent dominions. The partition was set out in the Indian Independence Act 1947 and ended the [[British Raj]]. It divided [[Bengal]] and the Punjab on the basis of district-wide non-Muslim or Muslim majorities, and split the British Indian Army, the railways and the central treasury between the two dominions. The rulers of princely states were released from their obligations to Britain and could accede to either dominion or remain independent. The partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people along religious lines. As of 2009, estimates of loss of life varied between two hundred thousand and two million. The two dominions came into existence at midnight on 14–15 August 1947. Hostility between [[India]] and [[Pakistan]] persisted afterward, and the secession of [[Bangladesh]] from Pakistan in 1971 was a later partition of Pakistan, not of India.

Three territorial divisions of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], 1772–1795. The partitions were conducted by the [[Habsburg monarchy]], the [[Kingdom of Prussia]] and the [[Russian Empire]]. The first was decided on 5 August 1772, after the Bar Confederation lost its war with Russia. The second, in 1793, followed the Polish–Russian War of 1792 and the Targowica Confederation; its treaty was signed at the Grodno Sejm on 23 January 1793, without Austria. The third, on 24 October 1795, followed the unsuccessful Kościuszko Uprising and ended the commonwealth, eliminating sovereign Poland and Lithuania for 123 years. After the [[Congress of Vienna]] in 1815, Austria established [[Galicia (Eastern Europe)|Galicia]], and Russia gained [[Warsaw]] from Prussia to form Congress Poland. The [[Treaty of Versailles]] allowed Poland's full independence to be restored after World War I.

Agreement in which parties cooperate to advance their mutual interests. Partners may be individuals, businesses, interest-based organizations, schools or governments. A partnership may involve issuing and holding equity, or it may be governed only by a [[Contract|contract]]. Medieval European merchants used the commenda, a form of partnership popular with Italian merchant bankers, to reward lenders despite church usury laws. According to a 2006 article, the first partnership was implemented in 1383 by Francesco di Marco Datini, a merchant of Prato and Florence. Cities of the [[Hanseatic League]] mutually supported each other's shipping, and Mongol elites, including the family of [[Marco Polo]], formed trade partnerships. In [[Common law|common law]] jurisdictions a written partnership agreement is not legally required, but partners benefit from one that sets out key terms.
